section.para: The MGED Socket Server provides a programmatic interface to MGED's geometry editing capabilities via Unix domain sockets. This interface enables external applications, scripts, and automation tools to execute geometry commands without requiring direct interaction with the MGED user interface.

The socket server was designed to support workflow automation, batch processing, and integration with external CAD/CAM systems. It implements a lightweight Unicode control character protocol that is language-agnostic and can be implemented in any programming language that supports Unix domain sockets.

Key features of the MGED Socket Server include:
Full access to all GED (Geometry EDitor) commands via a simple text protocol
Support for concurrent connections (up to 256 simultaneous clients)
Shared database access - all clients operate on the same geometry database instance
Non-blocking event-driven architecture with minimal performance overhead
Language-agnostic protocol suitable for C, Python, shell scripts, and other languages

To start MGED with the socket server enabled, use the -s option to specify the Unix domain socket path:
mged -c -a nu -s socket_path database.g

The -c option instructs MGED to use classic (non-GUI) mode, and -a nu attaches the NULL display manager to avoid requiring a graphical display. The -s option specifies where the Unix domain socket will be created in the filesystem.

Important considerations when starting the socket server:
Display Manager The NULL (nu) display manager is recommended for headless server deployments. Other display managers can be used if a graphical display is available.
Socket Path The socket path must be accessible to client processes. File system permissions control access to the socket.
Database File A database file must be specified. All socket clients will share access to this database instance.

Starting the MGED socket server is straightforward. From the operating system command line:
$ mged -c -a nu -s /tmp/mged.sock model.g BRL-CAD Release 7.x.x Geometry Editor (MGED) ... ATTACHING nu (Null Display Manager) mged>
The server is now running and listening for connections on /tmp/mged.sock. The MGED command prompt remains available for interactive use while the socket server operates in the background.

Clients connect to the server using standard Unix domain socket system calls. The socket path specified with -s must match the path used by clients. Once connected, clients can immediately begin sending commands.

The MGED Socket Server protocol uses Unicode control characters for message framing and field separation. This approach was chosen because control characters are rarely found in normal text, have single-byte UTF-8 encodings, and are standardized across platforms.

Three control characters from the C1 control block are used for protocol framing:
Character Hex Value Name Purpose
FS (␜) \x1C File Separator Message terminator - marks end of request or response
GS (␝) \x1D Group Separator Field separator - separates command/arguments and status/result/error
RS (␞) \x1E Record Separator Argument separator - separates individual command arguments
The Unicode symbols ␜, ␝, and ␞ shown in the table are visual representations for documentation purposes. Actual protocol messages use the literal control characters (\x1C, \x1D, \x1E).

Client requests follow this format:
<command>␝<arg1>␞<arg2>␞...␞<argN>␝
Breaking down the structure:
<command> The GED command name (e.g., "ls", "in", "kill", "units")
␝ Group Separator marking end of command and start of arguments
<arg1>␞<arg2>␞... Command arguments separated by Record Separator characters
␝ File Separator marking end of message (message terminator)

Example requests:
ls␝ (list database contents) units␝ (query current units) in␝sphere.s␞sph␞0␞0␞0␞5␝ (create sphere) opendb␝/path/to/model.g␝ (open database)

Server responses follow this format:
<status>␝<result>␝<error>␝
Response field definitions:
<status> Status code indicating success (OK) or error (ERR, ERR_PROTOCOL, etc.)
<result> Command output or result data (may be empty)
<error> Error message if status indicates failure (empty on success)

Example responses:
OK␝mm␝␝ (units command succeeded, result is "mm") OK␝sphere.s created␝␝ (object creation succeeded) ERR␝␝Unknown command: invalid␝ (command not recognized)

The server returns the following status codes:
Status Code Description
OK Command executed successfully. Result field contains command output.
ERR General command execution error. Error field contains details.
ERR_PROTOCOL Protocol violation (malformed request). Error field explains the issue.
ERR_NOMEM Memory allocation failure during request processing.
ERR_COMMAND Command execution failed. Error field contains command error message.
ERR_SYSTEM System-level error (I/O failure, etc.).
ERR_INTERNAL Internal server error. Should be rare; indicates a bug.

Client applications can be written in any language that supports Unix domain sockets. BRL-CAD includes a Python-based example client that demonstrates the protocol and provides an interactive debugging tool.

The examples/mged_socket_debug.py script provides a complete reference implementation of an MGED socket client. It demonstrates connection establishment, command formatting, response parsing, and error handling.

Key implementation points illustrated by the Python client:
Unix domain socket connection using socket.AF_UNIX
Proper insertion of control characters (\x1C, \x1D, \x1E) for message framing
Automatic message termination with FS character
Response parsing to extract status, result, and error fields
Visual representation of control characters for user display (␜, ␝, ␞)
Color-coded output for improved readability

Basic connection and command execution pattern in Python:
import socket
# Define protocol control characters FS = '\x1c' # File Separator (message terminator) GS = '\x1d' # Group Separator (field separator) RS = '\x1e' # Record Separator (argument separator)
# Connect to MGED socket server sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock.connect('/tmp/mged.sock')
# Send a simple command: "units" command = f"units{FS}" sock.send(command.encode('utf-8'))
# Receive response response = sock.recv(4096).decode('utf-8')
# Parse response (expected format: <status>␝<result>␝<error>␝) fields = response.rstrip(FS).split(GS) status = fields[0] if len(fields) > 0 else "" result = fields[1] if len(fields) > 1 else "" error = fields[2] if len(fields) > 2 else ""
if status == "OK": print(f"Success: {result}") else: print(f"Error: {error}")
sock.close()

For commands with multiple arguments, use the Record Separator to delimit them:
# Create a sphere at origin with radius 5 # Command: in sphere.s sph 0 0 0 5 command = f"in{GS}sphere.s{RS}sph{RS}0{RS}0{RS}0{RS}5{FS}" sock.send(command.encode('utf-8')) response = sock.recv(4096).decode('utf-8') # ... parse response as above ...

The complete mged_socket_debug.py example provides an interactive shell with special key bindings (Ctrl+G, Ctrl+R, Ctrl+F) to insert control characters, making it useful for testing and debugging protocol interactions.

A critical characteristic of the MGED Socket Server is that all clients share the same database instance. There is no per-client database isolation or copying. All socket clients, the MGED command-line interface, and any attached graphical display operate on a single shared ged database instance.

caution.para: Changes made through the socket interface are immediately visible to all other clients and to MGED's interactive interface. Conversely, changes made interactively in MGED are immediately visible to socket clients. There is no transaction isolation or rollback capability.

This shared-state model means that concurrent clients must coordinate their activities to avoid conflicts. For example, if one client deletes an object while another client is modifying it, the results are undefined and may be inconsistent.

section.para:
The shared database model provides several benefits:
Real-time collaboration - multiple users or processes can observe and manipulate the same geometry simultaneously
Memory efficiency - no duplication of potentially large geometry databases
Simplicity - no synchronization protocol needed between client views

The socket server is integrated into MGED's main event loop using a non-blocking, poll-based architecture. Socket I/O is checked periodically via the event_check() function, which uses poll() with a zero timeout to detect incoming connections and data without blocking.

This design ensures that:
The MGED interactive interface remains responsive while serving socket clients
Socket server overhead is minimal (typically <1ms per event loop iteration)
The server can handle multiple concurrent connections efficiently in a single thread
The server supports up to 256 concurrent client connections (defined by MGED_MAX_CLIENTS). This limit is sufficient for typical automation scenarios while keeping resource consumption bounded.

Commands received via the socket interface are executed using the generic ged_exec() function. This provides automatic support for all existing GED commands without requiring individual command bindings or wrappers.

When a command is received:
The request is parsed to extract the command name and arguments
ged_exec() is called with the parsed command and arguments
The command executes atomically - other clients cannot interrupt mid-execution
The result is captured from gedp->ged_result_str
A response is formatted and sent back to the client
This architecture means that any command available in MGED is automatically available via the socket interface, including future commands added to the GED library.

warning.para: The MGED Socket Server provides no authentication or authorization. Any process that can access the Unix domain socket file can connect and execute arbitrary GED commands with full privileges.
Access control is provided solely through filesystem permissions on the socket file. Ensure that the socket path is created in a directory with appropriate permissions to prevent unauthorized access.

section.para:
Security recommendations:
Create sockets in directories with restrictive permissions (e.g., mode 0700)
Use unique, unpredictable socket paths when multiple MGED instances run on the same system
Remove socket files when the server terminates (MGED does this automatically)
Do not expose socket paths to untrusted users or processes
Validate and sanitize command arguments in client code to prevent injection attacks

The socket server is designed for trusted environments where all clients are part of the same workflow or automation system. It is not suitable for untrusted or adversarial environments without additional security measures.

Start MGED with socket server:
$ mged -c -a nu -s /tmp/mged.sock model.g

From a Python client:
import socket
FS = '\x1c' sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock.connect('/tmp/mged.sock')
# Send "ls" command sock.send(f"ls{FS}".encode('utf-8'))
# Receive and display response response = sock.recv(4096).decode('utf-8') print(response)
sock.close()
Expected output:
OK␝_GLOBAL box1.s box2.r composite.c␝␝

Creating a sphere primitive:
import socket
FS = '\x1c' GS = '\x1d' RS = '\x1e'
sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock.connect('/tmp/mged.sock')
# Create sphere: in sphere.s sph 0 0 0 100 command = f"in{GS}sphere.s{RS}sph{RS}0{RS}0{RS}0{RS}100{FS}" sock.send(command.encode('utf-8'))
response = sock.recv(4096).decode('utf-8') fields = response.rstrip(FS).split(GS)
if fields[0] == "OK": print(f"Sphere created: {fields[1]}") else: print(f"Error: {fields[2]}")
sock.close()
Expected output:
Sphere created: sphere.s

Handling command errors:
import socket
FS = '\x1c' GS = '\x1d'
sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock.connect('/tmp/mged.sock')
# Try to execute an invalid command command = f"nonexistent_command{FS}" sock.send(command.encode('utf-8'))
response = sock.recv(4096).decode('utf-8') fields = response.rstrip(FS).split(GS)
status = fields[0] error = fields[2] if len(fields) > 2 else ""
if status.startswith("ERR"): print(f"Command failed with status: {status}") print(f"Error message: {error}")
sock.close()
Expected output:
Command failed with status: ERR Error message: nonexistent_command: command not found

Multiple clients can connect simultaneously. Changes made by one client are immediately visible to others:
# Client 1: Create an object import socket FS, GS, RS = '\x1c', '\x1d', '\x1e'
sock1 = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock1.connect('/tmp/mged.sock') sock1.send(f"in{GS}sphere1.s{RS}sph{RS}0{RS}0{RS}0{RS}50{FS}".encode('utf-8')) response1 = sock1.recv(4096).decode('utf-8')
# Client 2: List objects (will see sphere1.s created by Client 1) sock2 = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) sock2.connect('/tmp/mged.sock') sock2.send(f"ls{FS}".encode('utf-8')) response2 = sock2.recv(4096).decode('utf-8') # response2 will include "sphere1.s"
sock1.close() sock2.close()
